## Purpose

`EpiEstim` has been noted to have very narrow confidence intervals in certain 
situations. It was particularly noticed at periods of the COVID-19 pandemic 
when case rates were very high, so we wanted to investigate is there is a 
correlation between epidemic size and `EpiEstim` dispersion mis-calibration.

We used `EpiEstim` to estimate the instantaneous reproduction number from
simulated case counts, using different window sizes. The deterministic SIR model gives us a reference value
of $R_t$ for each day, which allows us to assess the uncertainty reported by
the estimator.

We varied population size while holding the shape of the epidemic curve and
the probability of observing a case fixed, and use the peak observed case count
to compare simulations with different numbers of cases available to the
estimator.

## 1. Simulation setup

We use a simple SIR model with known reproductive number dynamics. The true $R_t$ at each time point is analytically known:

$$R_t = R_0 \cdot \frac{S_t}{N}$$

The model is solved as a deterministic ODE on the proportion scale with
$R_0 = 2$, $\gamma = 1/5$ (a five-day infectious period) and a seed of
$10^{-4}$, over 100 days. Because $S_t$ is deterministic, $R_t = R_0 S_t$ is
exact at every time point: this is the ground truth against which `EpiEstim`
is scored. The incidence curve $\beta S_t I_t$ is the expected number of new
infections per capita per day, and is what the observation process below is
built on.

```{r}

sir_model = function(t, R0, g) {
  
  init <- c(S=1-1e-4, I=1e-4, R=0)
  parameters <- c(beta=R0 * g, gamma=g)
  time <- seq(0,t,length.out = t+1)
  
  eqn <- function(time,state,parameters){
    with(as.list(c(state,parameters)),{
      dS <- -beta*S*I
      dI <- beta*S*I-gamma*I
      dR <- gamma*I
      return(list(c(dS,dI,dR)))})
  }
  out = deSolve::ode(y=init,times=time,eqn,parms=parameters)
  out = as.data.frame(out)
  out %>% mutate(
    R_t = R0 * S,
    incid = parameters["beta"]*S*I
  )
  
}

tmp = sir_model(100, 2, 1/5)

ggplot(tmp, aes(x=time))+
  geom_line(aes(y=S,colour = "susceptible"))+
  geom_line(aes(y=I,colour = "infected"))+
  geom_line(aes(y=incid,colour = "new cases"))+
  geom_line(aes(y=R,colour = "recovered"))

ggplot(tmp, aes(x=time))+
  geom_line(
    aes(y=R_t,colour = "R_t")
    
  )

```

### Population sizes and observed counts

The population size `N` is swept over 100 log-spaced values from $10^{2.5}$
(about 320 people) to $10^{5}$, with 100 independent replicate runs at each,
giving 10000 scenarios. Expected daily cases are `incid * N`, and the observed
counts are a binomial thinning of those at a fixed ascertainment
probability `pObs = 0.5`.

Peak observed case count is the horizontal axis in the results. Each
combination of `run`, `N` and `pObs` defines one simulated epidemic, one
`EpiEstim` fit and one row of scores.

```{r}
scenarios = tidyr::crossing(
  N = round(10 ^ seq(2.5,5,length.out=100)),
  pObs = 0.5, #c(0.2, 0.8),
  run = 1:100
) %>% 
  dplyr::cross_join(tmp) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    cases = round(incid*N),
    obs = rbinom(dplyr::n(), cases, pObs)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(run,N,pObs) %>%
  dplyr::glimpse()

# ggplot(scenarios, aes(x=time, group=run))+
#   facet_grid(as.factor(N) ~ as.factor(pObs), scales = "free")+
#   geom_step(aes(y=obs))
  
```

## 2. Estimating $R_t$ with EpiEstim

We fitted `EpiEstim` to the observed counts over a random window between the 25th
and 75th simulation day in each scenario using 2, 4, 7, 10, and 14 day windows, 
a parametric serial interval with mean of 5 and
standard deviation both 5 days (matching that o the simulation), and a prior on
$R_t$ with mean of 2 (matching the simulation R0) and a standard deviation of 5.

For each window we used the posterior mean and standard deviation to
parametrise a Gamma distribution, scored against the reference $R_t$ at
the window end. We used a log link for the bias adjustment. For each population
size 100 time-series of daily observed new cases were randomly sampled from the model 
assuming ascertainment of 0.5 using a binomial. There was no observation delay.

```{r}

results = scenarios %>% dplyr::group_modify(function(d,g,...) {
  
  # Every group (i.e. 10000 groups, 100 runs of the same simulation in different population sizes)
  # has three EpiEstim estimates at the same random time during days 25-75 the simulation. 
  # with different window widths.
  endpoint = sample(50-14,1) + 14 +25
  starts = endpoint-c(2,4,7,10,14)
  ends = rep(endpoint,length(starts))
  
  ee = suppressWarnings(EpiEstim::estimate_R(
    incid = data.frame(I = d$obs),
    method = "parametric_si",
    config = EpiEstim::make_config(
      method = "parametric_si",
      mean_si = 5, std_si = 5,
      t_start = starts, t_end = ends,
      mean_prior = 2, std_prior = 5
    )
  ))
  
  tmp = d %>% 
    # filter(obs>0) %>% 
    inner_join(
      ee$R %>% 
        mutate(window = t_end-t_start) %>%
        select(time = t_end, window=window, mean=`Mean(R)`, sd = `Std(R)`), 
      by = "time"
    )
  
  return(tmp)
  
})
```


## 3. Scoring

`prediction_scores()` is applied per scenario. `max_obs`, the peak observed
case count, is computed inside the scenario grouping before the regroup, so it
indexes the scenario rather than being recomputed over a pooled set. The
threshold of 1 is the epidemiologically meaningful one: it asks how often the
prediction is on the wrong side of "the epidemic is growing".

We set `calibration` to `NA` because the spread-to-error ratio of the
`EpiEstim` estimates is unknown.

```{r}

tmp = scenarios %>% dplyr::group_by(N,pObs) %>% dplyr::summarise(max_obs = max(obs))

scores = results %>%
  dplyr::transmute(
    window,
    true_value= R_t, location = mean, scale = sd, link="log", dist="gamma2",
    calibration=NA_real_
  ) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(N, pObs, dist, link, calibration, window) %>%
  prediction_scores(threshold = 1) %>% 
  dplyr::inner_join(tmp, by=c("N","pObs"))


plotdata = scores %>% ungroup() %>% mutate(
  H0_B_pit = b_pit_significance(B_pit = B_pit, n_predictions = n_predictions) %>% pull(p_value) > 0.05,
  H0_U_pit = u_pit_significance(U_pit = U_pit, n_predictions = n_predictions) %>% pull(p_value) > 0.05,
  H0_D_pit = d_pit_significance(D_pit = D_pit, n_predictions = n_predictions) %>% pull(p_value) > 0.05,
  `P(obs)`=as.factor(pObs),
  window = as.factor(window)
  # timing = cut(time, c(-Inf,30,60,Inf), labels=c("growth","peak","resolution"))
)

signif = tibble(
  n_predictions = 100,
  B_crit = b_pit_significance(B_pit = NA, n_predictions = n_predictions),
  U_crit = u_pit_significance(U_pit = NA, n_predictions = n_predictions),
  D_crit = d_pit_significance(D_pit = NA, n_predictions = n_predictions)
)
```

```{r}
.gg_save_as(
```

### Interpretation

`EpiEstim` tended to overestimate $R_t$ across the epidemic sizes studied
regardless of epidemic size (panel A) but with more effect with larger windows.
Three possible contributing factors are the prior with mean of 2 and standard
deviation of 5, the lag from estimating a falling $R_t$ at the end of the
window, and the impact of a day zero truncation of the generation time
distribution enforced by `EpiEstim`. `EpiEstim` assumes a constant $R_t$ during
the window which would intuitively make it more likely to overestimate due to
lag, in our scenario of a monotonically falling $R_t$, and for that to 
be related to window size.

The baseline score $B_pit$ (lower is better) suggests `EpiEstim` with smaller 
windows is overall better and suggests its performance worsens in large epidemics
(panel B). This is largely mirroring the bias. The vast majority of the estimators 
are statistically unlikely to be well calibrated (dashed line is critical 0.95 
threshold for 100 estimates).

The mean directed score $D_pit$ adjusts for bias, (panel C). The negative scores indicate intervals
that were too wide at low counts (excessively conservative), and the positive scores indicate
intervals that were too narrow at high counts (overconfident). `EpiEstim` with a
2 day window is conservative unless used in epidemics with a case count of over 1000. This
is most likely reflecting reversion to the under-confident prior, and longer
windows show this reversion is resolved in epidemics with smaller case counts. 
Large amounts of over-confidence are exhibited by `EpiEstim` at all windows in
larger epidemics and this is clearly correlated with window size. 

The undirected score reached its minimum at different epidemic sizes depending on
window size (panel D) and epidemic size. It is likely that adjusting the window 
size depending on the size of the epidemic could result in well calibrated 
estimates from `EpiEstim`.

With $n = 100$ scored predictions per scenario, the reference expressions used in
this comparison are $D^*_{pit} \sim N(0, 1/48n)$ and
$\mathbb{E}[U^*_{pit}] = \sqrt{2\pi}/(8\sqrt{n})$. 

```{r}

  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se=TRUE)+
  scale_x_log10()+
  xlab("peak observed case count")+

  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype="solid")

p6c = ggplot(plotdata, aes(x=max_obs, colour = window,y=mean_coverage.0.5_adj))+
  geom_point()+
  geom_smooth(se=TRUE)+
  scale_x_log10()+
```

REWRITE: **CRPS runs the other way.** Panel A falls monotonically from 0.183 to 0.087
(correlation $-0.89$ with $\log_{10}$ peak cases). Read without care it says
that the bigger the epidemic, the better the forecast. What it is actually
measuring is sharpness: in a large epidemic the posterior is narrow, so the
score is small even as calibration deteriorates. $D^*_{pit}$ is monotone in
the opposite direction (correlation $+0.91$) and is the only metric in the
panel that identifies the large-epidemic forecasts as the mis-calibrated ones.
This is the central argument of the paper, made on a real estimator rather
than a constructed example: a proper score and a dispersion diagnostic can
rank the same forecaster in opposite directions, and they are answering
different questions.

REWRITE: Coverage corroborates the PIT-Wasserstein reading and not the CRPS one.
Nominal 95% intervals cover 91% of true values in the smallest epidemics and
only 51% in the largest; nominal 50% intervals fall from 0.44 to 0.29. The
estimator is getting worse by the only criterion that asks whether its stated
uncertainty is honest.


### Caveats

This experiment identifies *that* the dispersion calibration changes sign with
epidemic size; it does not separate the contributions of the Gamma prior, and 
any genuine over-confidence in the renewal-equation
likelihood. Disentangling those would need a prior 
sensitivity sweep and is out of scope here.
